newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. says no progress in port dispute with Japan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says no progress in port dispute with Japan.

text.p: The United States said on Wednesday it had not seen any progress in its dispute with Japan over Japanese port practices, despite the threat of imminent U.S. sanctions.

The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) announced plans to impose sanctions on three Japanese shipping firms in November. The announcement was followed by a 60-day comment period which ended on January 20.
A U.S. embassy official said the FMC was still considering those comments, although a decision was expected "very soon".
He also said he believed the dispute could be resolved without the use of sanctions but declined to comment on details of talks between Japanese and foreign shippers held on Wednesday.

The FMC, angry at what it says are costly and discriminatory port practices, is considering slapping a $100,000 surcharge on Japan's top ship operators Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha, and Nippon Yusen KK every time they stop at a U.S. port.

The FMC has charged that Japan's Transport Ministry discourages applications for cargo handling licences and that the oversight of the Japan Harbour and Transport Authority (JHTA) in all vessel operations, no matter how minor, gives the JHTA effective control of port business in Japan.
"What we don't like is a system which supports allocations of services, which is essentially a cartel," the official said of the JHTA.

Washington says Japanese port costs are the highest in the world, up to three to five times greater than other ports in Asia. If changes were made, port costs could be reduced by as much as 20 percent, the official said.
The three Japanese shipping firms have complained to the FMC, arguing that the sanctions, if imposed, would cost them 5 billion yen ($40.9 million) a year.

The Transport Ministry says that newcomers have been restricted in the past because of a surplus of stevedores and pledged to lift restrictions on port service licences within three to five years. However the United States says that this is not fast enough.
